item.title: Object Classification
item.content:encoded:
Keter, perhaps?

As asked before, is it possible for SCP-676 to consume the planet if not continuously sated? The SCP also does not pass the "locked box" test very well, given the fact that it cannot be contained in a laboratory setting. In fact, containing it requires a continuous resource which may not always be readily available.

It will hit the river. If that dries up, maybe a lake. Then, the lake may become affected with the dissolving trait, while slowly being drained. And if it expands to include an ocean… well, think about it. That's an ocean that dissolves everything that comes into contact with it. There's no way to tell if the water being drained is recirculated back out, or simply… vanishing.

There's no known limit to this thing, is what I'm getting at. XK-Class end-of-the-world scenario?

item.content:encoded: That's what I love about this one too. The containment procedure is completely illogical and the effect is completely impossible. Yet there it is, existing anyway. It grows if you stop adding to it but stays stable if you let the water keep pouring in. It's not actively trying to kill you, it doesn't make you crazy or hypnotize you, but if that spring ever dries up I could imagine this thing devouring the entire planet.

For the first, that's what I was getting at. If radioactive labels get chewed up, you know something odd's going on.

For the second, I'm sure the Foundation has done something like that (maybe without the D-class). The thing is, even if you pull up a quick cupful, it still disintegrates everything, so you wouldn't be able to perform any useful tests, so there was nothing worth mentioning in the brief that was learned. Or at least that's how I approached it. If we think we need to mention that we can.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Dyes and radioactively labeled markers disappear as well, suggesting that the process occurs below the chemical level.

Chemical, nothing — if radioactive markers disappear, that's subatomic disintegration. This thing is dangerous.

As a result it has proven impossible to take and retain samples from SCP-676’s basin, and it is unknown if the fluid is water or another colorless liquid compound.

Easy way to check: give a D-class a glass of the stuff and see what happens. Surely it doesn't disintegrate things so quickly that you couldn't hold a glass of it for a moment…?
